title: Chapter 15.  Old Status vs New Status — A Direct Constitutional & Administrative Comparison

blocks.content: This chapter consolidates Chapters 9-14 into a single, direct side-by-side comparison table — precisely the format most useful for rapid exam revision of J&K's 'old' (pre-August 2019) versus 'new' (post-October 2019) constitutional and administrative status.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Provides a comprehensive old-vs-new comparison of constitutional and administrative status.
Outlines the specific institutional features and legal provisions that remain unchanged.
Summarizes key revision points essential for quick exam review.

blocks.content: Old Status vs New Status — A Direct Constitutional & Administrative Comparison

cells: Feature
OLD Status (Pre-Aug 2019)
NEW Status (Post-Oct 2019)
Constitutional category
State of Jammu and Kashmir (with special status under Article 370)
Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir (with Legislative Assembly) — a structurally distinct, separate UT of Ladakh (without Assembly) also created
Applicability of Indian Constitution
Only Article 1 and Article 370 applied automatically; other provisions applied selectively via Presidential Orders requiring state concurrence
Entire Constitution of India applies fully and directly, as in any other Indian state/UT
Separate state Constitution
Yes — J&K's own Constitution (adopted 1957) governed matters outside the Indian Constitution's limited applicability
No — no separate Constitution; governed entirely under the Constitution of India and the Reorganisation Act, 2019
Permanent Resident/property rights (Article 35A)
Only 'Permanent Residents' could buy land/property or hold permanent state jobs; other Indian citizens could not
Article 35A inoperative; land/property purchase restrictions substantially removed; a broader 'domicile' category governs local job/benefit eligibility
Head of the territory
Governor (a title that itself replaced the earlier 'Sadar-i-Riyasat', per Chapter 9)
Lieutenant Governor
Legislature's law-making power
State legislature had wide autonomous law-making power except on the originally acceded subjects (Defence, External Affairs, Communications) plus subsequently extended Union/Concurrent subjects

UT Assembly (since restored, Chapter 16) legislates on subjects allocated to UTs-with-Assembly under Article 239A, generally narrower than full state powers, with the LG retaining significant reserved powers (broadly comparable in structure to Delhi's framework, covered in the companion Delhi GS volume)
State/UT flag
J&K had its own separate state flag, used alongside the Indian national flag
No separate flag; only the Indian national flag is used
Criminal law
Separate Ranbir Penal Code and related procedural codes applied
Central criminal codes (as applicable across India) apply
Rajya Sabha/Lok Sabha representation
J&K state sent representatives to both Houses as any state would
J&K UT continues to send Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members; representation levels adjusted per the Reorganisation Act and subsequent delimitation
Reservation policy
State-specific reservation framework operated largely independently of central norms
Central SC/ST/OBC/EWS reservation norms extended, alongside specific J&K border-area reservation categories

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: This single table is the highest-yield revision resource in the entire book for J&K's constitutional-status questions — most direct 'old vs new' exam questions can be answered by mapping the specific feature asked about (flag, Constitution, land rights, legislature, etc.) onto this comparison.

items: J&K's geography, mountain ranges, rivers, climate zones and physical landscape (Chapters 1-4) are, of course, entirely unaffected by the constitutional reorganisation — a useful reminder that not every aspect of the region's 'status' changed in 2019.

J&K's cultural heritage, major religious/pilgrimage sites, language traditions, and historical monuments (covered in Chapters 20-21) similarly remain unaffected by the administrative and constitutional changes, continuing under their own separate frameworks of protection and promotion.

The region's fundamental geopolitical position — bordered by Pakistan across the LoC, with the underlying international dispute over the former princely state's status unresolved — also remains structurally unchanged by India's internal constitutional reorganisation, even as India's official position treats the entire matter as a fully settled internal constitutional question.

This chapter is a pure revision-consolidation chapter — see the master comparison table above for rapid old-vs-new recall across all major features (Constitution, flag, land rights, head of territory, legislature, criminal law, reservation policy).
Geography, culture, heritage and religious sites are unaffected by the 2019 constitutional reorganisation.
The underlying India-Pakistan international dispute over the former princely state's status remains unresolved, separate from India's internal constitutional changes.
